description: Final-year Computer Systems Engineering student building an astronaut health monitoring tool. Plan: a web dashboard that tracks health indicators over time and uses anomaly detection to flag early warning signs. I will handle backend, AI and data. Looking for a frontend or UI designer, someone who can write and present the story, and someone who can research astronaut health data. We have little time, so we will keep the scope small and finish a working demo.
summary: Project Astra Vitals presents AstroHealth, a web app that helps astronauts monitor six health indicators during long space missions. Users log daily readings, explore charts and a clickable body map, and receive guidance when readings change from their personal baseline. A simulated 180-day Mars transit demonstrates health changes linked to spaceflight hazards. Across 40 synthetic missions, personal-baseline monitoring flagged drifts detected by both methods 4.7 days earlier on average than fixed ranges, with more quiet-day flags. NASA Human Research Program resources inform the hazard explanations. Guidance only, not a medical diagnosis.
details:
AstroHealth tracks heart rate, systolic blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood. Users enter daily readings, explore trends and a clickable body map, and receive simple guidance.

The first 14 entries establish a personal baseline. From entry 15, an exponentially weighted moving average helps identify persistent changes. Fixed demo ranges can also trigger alerts. Entries are saved locally in the browser; a separate simulated sample is available.

Across 40 simulated 180-day missions, the baseline method detected 240 of 240 injected indicator drifts versus 200 for fixed ranges. For drifts detected by both, mean lead time was 4.7 days. Quiet indicator-day flag rates were 4.2% versus 0.2%. These are synthetic results, not clinical validation.

NASA Human Research Program resources informed our hazard explanations. The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Recharts. Reference ranges are illustrative; the app does not measure radiation or provide medical diagnosis.
